title: The path, closed
hookLine: eight factors, walked together, not one after another

cards: A wheel doesn't turn one spoke at a time. Forty-eight days ago, this stretch opened with a wheel of eight spokes, and the nun Dhammadinna sorting them into three trainings.

Since then the spokes have come out one by one: view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, concentration. That's how you learn a list. But the suttas don't describe walking the path that way.
Today the spokes go back in.

teach.b: Here they are once more: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration.

Dhammadinna showed how they sort into virtue, concentration and wisdom. The Great Forty, MN 117, shows how they feed each other. In one who has right view, the Buddha says, right intention comes into being.

teach.h: EACH FACTOR GIVES RISE TO THE NEXT.
teach.b: From right intention, right speech; from right speech, right action; from right action, right livelihood; and on down the line, each factor giving rise to the next, as far as right concentration.
Then the sutta keeps going: from right concentration, right knowledge, and from right knowledge, right liberation.

teach.h: TEN FOR THE ONE WHO HAS ARRIVED.
teach.b: Eight factors for one in training; ten for one who has arrived. The same sutta has view, effort and mindfulness running around each of the others, so the chain isn't a ladder you climb once.
Nobody finishes right view before starting right speech. You speak a little more carefully, and your view clears a little.
Your view clears, and your work changes. Your work changes, and the mind gathers more easily. The Dhammapada says it in one line, in Max Müller's translation: “The best of ways is the eightfold.”
The Pali word for path, magga, is the ordinary word for a road. And nobody walks a road with all the left steps first. Both feet, the whole way.

how: Buddhists across schools teach the eight factors as three trainings, virtue, concentration and wisdom, developed together rather than in sequence; the eight-spoked wheel is widely used as a symbol of the teaching.

o: a single practice that replaces all the others
eight factors walked together, each feeding the rest
eight steps climbed in order, one after another

p: path: the ordinary word for a road

s: the eight factors are mastered strictly in order, one by one
they're walked together; each strengthens the others.
in MN 117, the chain stops at right concentration
it goes on to right knowledge and right liberation: ten factors for one who has arrived.
in MN 44, a nun explains the path's three trainings
Dhammadinna, and the Buddha says he'd have answered the same.

games.q: in MN 117, the Buddha says one factor leads the way for the others. which one?
games.why: right view comes first. in one with right view, right intention comes into being, and so on down the line, each factor giving rise to the next.

practice: Let the eight pass through, one breath each: view, seeing things as they are; intention, goodwill; speech, today's words; action, harming no one; livelihood, your work; effort, the good you keep going; mindfulness, this breath; concentration, gathered here.
Then let go of the list, and sit with all eight at once, nothing left out.

wordCard.voice: The path. Eight factors, walked together like the spokes of one wheel, each one strengthening the rest.

orig.note: Pali ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo: the noble eightfold path; aṅga means a limb or factor, not a step.

carryVoice: Your line: eight together. Each one, walked, makes the others easier. Four hundred days; see you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 44, Culavedalla Sutta (Dhammadinna and the three trainings)
Majjhima Nikaya 117, Mahacattarisaka Sutta (right view comes first)

sources.q: The best of ways is the eightfold
